assessment: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are a class of antibiotics that are inspired by natural components of innate immunity, which raises the specter of bacteria becoming resistant to both. Jangir et al. test this idea and find compelling evidence that a plasmid that encodes resistance to the AMP colistin also increases resistance to AMPs produced by humans, pigs, and chickens, enables the bacteria to grow better in low levels of AMP, and increases bacterial virulence in an insect model of infection. This important study will be of interest to both evolutionary biologists and microbiologists focused on antimicrobial therapy and suggests that the evolution of resistance to these compounds can have collateral effects on immune evasion as well.
